This week, I had the honor of spending time with Lincoln and Parker Moss, and their truly amazing mom Kelly.  They drove from Salem to our nation’s Capitol to tell me about their beloved brother and son, Weston Moss.

Weston was 12. A proud Boy Scout. Loved Super Mario and Legos. Dreamed of designing games at Nintendo. He was an artist who shared his beautiful art with the world.

For his 11th birthday, Weston skipped presents and instead donated 500 LEGO sets to kids fighting cancer at the Jimmy Fund Clinic.

Even while battling a rare bone cancer called Ewing Sarcoma, Wes never stopped thinking of other kids in the fight. In his final days, he had one more wish: that we carry on his mission of ending cancer as we know it and making life better for everyone one of us who is blessed to be living it. 

That’s how Weston’s Big Wish was born.

This morning, I was in Salem with Weston’s amazingly resilient dad James and his loving grandmother Donna at the Salem Lions Race Against Childhood Cancer — neighbors, some meeting the Moss family for the first time, showing up for a truly remarkable boy who gave his all to others.

That’s the living legacy and blessed soul of Weston Moss. That’s Salem. That’s New Hampshire. 

I will never stop fighting to make Weston’s Big Wish a reality: more federal funding for research, kinder treatments, and more joy for every kid facing what Wes faced.

May God bless Weston Moss and the entire Moss family.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​ 🙏

This week, I had the honor of spending time with Lincoln and Parker Moss, and their truly amazing mom Kelly.  They drove from Salem to our nation’s Capitol to tell me about their beloved brother and son, Weston Moss.

Weston was 12. A proud Boy Scout. Loved Super Mario and Legos. Dreamed of designing games at Nintendo. He was an artist who shared his beautiful art with the world.

For his 11th birthday, Weston skipped presents and instead donated 500 LEGO sets to kids fighting cancer at the Jimmy Fund Clinic.

Even while battling a rare bone cancer called Ewing Sarcoma, Wes never stopped thinking of other kids in the fight. In his final days, he had one more wish: that we carry on his mission of ending cancer as we know it and making life better for everyone one of us who is blessed to be living it. 

That’s how Weston’s Big Wish was born.

This morning, I was in Salem with Weston’s amazingly resilient dad James and his loving grandmother Donna at the Salem Lions Race Against Childhood Cancer — neighbors, some meeting the Moss family for the first time, showing up for a truly remarkable boy who gave his all to others.

That’s the living legacy and blessed soul of Weston Moss. That’s Salem. That’s New Hampshire. 

I will never stop fighting to make Weston’s Big Wish a reality: more federal funding for research, kinder treatments, and more joy for every kid facing what Wes faced.

May God bless Weston Moss and the entire Moss family.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​ 🙏

Every year, nearly 21,000 families in our country tragically lose a child to stillbirth. While dealing with this loss, these families not only have to grapple with grief, but also make difficult financial decisions to cover medical costs, funeral expenses, and much more during one of their darkest moments. On National Stillbirth Prevention and Awareness Day, we recognize the families who lost their children far too soon and the challenges they face for years to come.

That’s why during my time in the Maryland Senate, I introduced a bill to ensure Maryland families have the time and resources to properly honor their child, rather than worrying about their finances during one of their most challenging moments. I’m grateful that bill has finally passed this year thanks to the tireless work of Senator Waldstreicher and my state partners.

Getting the spent nuclear fuel off our coastline has been a top priority of mine for as long as I've served in Congress, and it will stay that way for as long as it takes. There is no question that this fuel needs to move as quickly and safely as possible.

When I got to Congress in 2019, there was no plan to move it. 

The federal government was supposed to start taking this waste in 1998 and never did. 

Yucca Mountain, the only site Congress ever picked, was shut down in 2009, and nothing replaced it. Months before I took office, a canister nearly fell 18 feet during loading. In sum, I inherited a bad situation.

One of my first steps was bringing experts and community leaders together on a SONGS Task Force. They presented findings and recommendations that have guided my work ever since.

I brought Democrats and Republicans together in the Spent Nuclear Fuel Solutions Caucus to restart a stalled national conversation. I’ve met regularly with Department of Energy staff, including earlier this week, to discuss the new path forward.

Through the House Appropriations process, I've helped secure over $250 million for this work. 

That includes Atlas, a new railcar built to carry spent fuel safely across the country by rail. The funding we secured supported the last administration's work to find willing host communities through a collaborative siting program. It also is assisting the new Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses, a continuation of this work, with six states already signing up.

I’ve also introduced several pieces of bipartisan legislation that provide a strong roadmap for the future, including language to prioritize the movement of spent fuel from sites like ours, and to create a new sole purpose entity for the management of spent fuel nationwide.

There is much work ahead, but I’m greatly encouraged by our progress. 

I'll be sharing a more comprehensive update in coming weeks.

Last night, I voted for the bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act, legislation I cosponsored, to help protect South Texas families and small businesses from paying the electricity infrastructure costs created by large data centers.

The principle is simple: if a project creates the cost, the project should pay the cost.
